headline: Southington fire department wins $3.03 million staffing grant, but town approval is still pending
dek: The FEMA award could add 12 firefighters and expand around-the-clock coverage, but the Town Council must still accept the grant and decide how to pay for the positions after federal support ends.
body: Southington’s fire department has been awarded a $3.03 million federal grant that could add 12 firefighters to the department, a potentially significant change for a town that has relied on a mix of career staff, volunteers and mutual aid from neighboring communities. The award was announced by the department in late September and reported locally this week, but it is not yet a hiring authorization: the Town Council must review and accept the grant before the plan can move forward.

The money comes through the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Staffing for Adequate Fire and Emergency Response program, commonly called SAFER. FEMA describes SAFER as a competitive grant program intended to help fire departments increase the number of firefighters, meet minimum staffing standards and achieve 24-hour coverage. Its guidance says hiring awards can support the traditional missions of fire departments as well as stronger protection from fire and related hazards. [FEMA’s SAFER program guidance](https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_gpd-fy-2023-safer-faqs.pdf) provides that broader context.

Southington officials and department representatives say the local award would address a long-running staffing problem. The Southington Outsider reported that the department’s volunteer ranks have fallen from more than 100 people about 14 years ago to roughly 20 now, according to Captain Daniel Comen, who wrote the grant application. That decline has left the station at 35 Clark Street staffed only on weekdays, the publication reported. The new grant is intended to make that station available around the clock.

The operational goal is more than adding names to a roster. Comen told the Southington Outsider that the department now has as many as seven firefighters on duty and can fall to six, while the grant-supported plan would raise the regular daily level to 11, with a low point of 10. The department says that additional coverage could make it easier to send a crew to an emergency without leaving another station short-handed.

The department also expects the staffing change to reduce its dependence on neighboring towns for routine coverage. Southington currently calls on mutual-aid partners in Meriden, Bristol, New Britain, Plainville and Cheshire when it needs to maintain station coverage while responding to a larger fire, according to Comen’s account in the Southington Outsider. He said the department’s goal is to reduce routine mutual-aid requests by about half. That is a department target, not a guaranteed result of the award, and actual response times will depend on hiring, training, scheduling and call volume.

The award is unusually large by the department’s accounting. Southington Fire Department officials told Patch that it was the only fiscal-year 2025 SAFER award announced for a Connecticut department at the time, the largest announced in New England, the second-largest in the Northeast and the 11th-largest nationally. Those rankings are based on awards announced so far, rather than a permanent ranking of every fire department or a measure of fire outcomes. The Quinnipiac Post reported the same pending-review status and described the award as one of the largest in the region based on the department’s figures.

The unresolved issue is what happens after the federal grant period. Patch reported that the award would offset the cost of hiring the 12 firefighters, but that local officials and taxpayers would ultimately have to decide whether to keep funding the positions when federal money runs out. The Southington Outsider also reported that the department expects the added staffing to reduce overtime costs, but potential savings do not by themselves establish the town’s future payroll obligation. The town has not yet announced a final implementation schedule or long-term cost decision.

The next formal checkpoint is the Town Council’s review and acceptance of the grant. Patch reported that the council’s next regular meeting is scheduled for Oct. 12 at the John Weichsel Municipal Center, while the Southington Outsider reported that the department expected the grant to be considered at a meeting on Oct. 13. The differing dates show why the agenda and the council’s official action should be checked before treating the award as final. Until the council acts, Southington has a federal staffing opportunity, not 12 newly hired firefighters.
author: NorthEast News Desk
